transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-08
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (CTO - Riverbend), Sana Patel (ML Eng), Diego Ruiz (DevOps)

Summary:
Quick recap of last week's soak, review of throughput numbers, tuning knobs (continuous batching, concurrency targets, queue watermarking), and next steps for canary and dedicated cost estimate. Some audio glitches; a few words mis-transcribed (e.g., K-V cash for KV cache).

Topics covered:
- Soak run results (p50/p95, tokens/sec, avg batch size)
- Queue/backpressure behavior and target queue depth
- Concurrency targets and trade-offs (latency vs throughput)
- Batch sizing and adaptive batching heuristics
- Fallback model variants and burst capacity policy
- Next steps (benchmarks, configs, cost)

[00:00] Avery Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick roll call, then we'll jump into the numbers from the 24-hour soak we ran over the weekend.
[00:14] Marcus Lee: Hey, Marcus here. Sana and Diego are on as well.
[00:17] Sana Patel: Yep, hi.
[00:19] Diego Ruiz: Morning.
[00:21] Priya Raman: Priya from Redwood, hi all. Alright, Avery, want me to share the dashboard?
[00:26] Avery Chen: Please, that would be perfect. Full disclaimer, the dashboard has some synthetic labels — we had a minor naming clash so some metrics are under old keys.
[01:02] Priya Raman: (screen) Ok, Top-left, the 24h soak: average tokens/sec peaked at 3,200 during steady periods, with p50 latency ~120ms and p95 ~540ms. Average batch size around 11.8, KV cache hit rate recorded at 28% but that's counting only prefix hits, we sketched a change that should push that up.
[01:35] Marcus Lee: That p95 is higher than we expected at the higher concurrencies. We saw occasional tail spikes up to ~1.2s.
[01:42] Priya Raman: Yeah, the tail correlates with concurrent bursts where queue depth spikes above ~45 requests. The continuous batching window was defaulted to 30ms, which yields decent batches but increases head-of-line contention under burst.
[02:05] Sana Patel: Can you explain head-of-line contention again? I think we saw that word in the writeup but, uh, lost it.
[02:10] Priya Raman: Sure. So if one large request sits at the front of the FIFO queue it prevents the small ones behind it from being batched/processed quickly — the runtime will often wait for the batching window to close to maximize batch size, but that waiting can hurt latency for some requests.
[02:34] Diego Ruiz: Makes sense. Network-wise we saw very few retransmits, so this looks serving-side.
[02:40] Priya Raman: Right. Two levers: 1) tighten the batching window (e.g., 10ms) to reduce waiting, 2) implement adaptive batching that flushes when queue depth or time thresholds hit.
[03:05] Avery Chen: Quick numbers proposal: target steady concurrency of 12 workers for production — that gave us a good tokens/sec to latency tradeoff in the tests. When we pushed to concurrency 24, tokens/sec increased only marginally to ~3,800 but p95 jumped to ~900ms and instability crept in.
[03:35] Marcus Lee: So 12 is our baseline target. What about peak spikes? Our SLA needs 99.5% under 800ms.
[03:45] Priya Raman: For spikes we'd suggest configuring a burst band: allow temporary concurrency ramp to 18 with autoscaling and a fallback policy that routes to the quantized-4bit model if p95 exceeds 800ms or error rate climbs. That way user-visible latency stays bounded.
[04:10] Sana Patel: Is the quantized variant audited for quality? We have a fighting set in evals — we can run ASAP.
[04:16] Avery Chen: Yes, we ran a small eval sweep; most cases within acceptable delta, some long-context summarization had quality drift. We'll share the eval report.
[04:30] Marcus Lee: Also curious about the KV cache — you mentioned a change that could boost hits.
[04:36] Priya Raman: Right, currently prefix caching is conservative; we're proposing a more aggressive prefix match threshold and integrating a short-term local LRU to capture repeated prefixes in the same session. We estimate hit rate could go from 28% to ~60%. Even modest KV hit gains reduce tokens/sec by ~15-20% and reduce latency tails.
[05:05] Diego Ruiz: That's significant. Any infra caveats? Memory, eviction?
[05:09] Priya Raman: We'll size cache per-GPU with a 512MB suggestion for your long-context workloads; eviction policy will be LRU with sticky entries for 30 minutes. We'll share the config snippet.
[05:26] [crosstalk]
[05:30] Avery Chen: Next, queue watermarking — we saw queue depth crossing 60 in a few bursts which correlated strongly with tail latency. We recommend setting a watermark at 40 requests. That will trigger early flushing/backpressure into a shallow queue or route to fallback.
[05:55] Marcus Lee: If we set watermark 40 do we risk dropping requests?
[05:58] Priya Raman: No, we won't drop. We'll surface backpressure upstream — Redwood's router can signal 429s for non-critical paths or route to lower-cost-but-slower model. The goal is graceful degradation.
[06:18] Sana Patel: For our test, can we see the effect with synthetic traffic that mirrors our peak waveform? We have a weekday spike pattern and a daily lull.
[06:26] Priya Raman: Yes, please share the traffic waveform sample and timezones — we'll replicate in the micro-bench.
[06:33] Avery Chen: I'll attach the micro-benchmark script to the follow-up; it's a small Go binary that replays tokenized requests and supports waveform injection.
[06:45] Marcus Lee: Good. Cost question — running with concurrency 12 vs 18 what's the hit?
[06:51] Priya Raman: Very rough ballpark: concurrency 12 steady cost X, 18 ~1.35X, 24 ~1.6X factoring GPU utilization and model variants. We'll formalize and send a delta table for Hosted vs Dedicated.
[07:09] Diego Ruiz: Any recommended SLA knobs for us while we test?
[07:12] Priya Raman: Enable detailed tracing for the canary: per-token latency histograms, batch-size distribution, queue depth timeline. Keep sampling at 100% for 1 hour, then drop to 5%.
[07:30] Sana Patel: About the adaptive batching, what heuristics do you use? Time, queue depth, request size?
[07:36] Priya Raman: All three. We recommend a primary time window (start 12ms), queue depth threshold (flush if >=40), and a size-aware flush (if a request is over 1,500 tokens flush immediately). This reduces head-of-line for large requests.
[07:58] Marcus Lee: In the soak logs we saw a recurring pattern at 03:00 PST where a forklift job hit the cluster — that probably explains the spike.
[08:06] Diego Ruiz: Yeah, our nightly ETL kicks off and sometimes calls internal inference for classification, didn't think it would show up there. We'll separate that traffic into a different route.
[08:15] Avery Chen: Good call. Route isolation is a nice operational step — keep user-facing traffic isolated from internal batch calls.
[08:25] Priya Raman: Also flagged: the client-side retry backoff wasn't jittered, which caused accidental synchronized retries during failures. Please add jittered exponential backoff to avoid thundering herd.
[08:40] Sana Patel: We'll patch that.
[08:44] [15:00 min mark summary noise]
[15:05] Priya Raman: Jumping ahead, test results when we enabled aggressive KV prefix caching in the dev run: tokens/sec dropped by ~17% and p95 improved from 540ms -> 370ms at concurrency 12. That's promising.
[15:28] Marcus Lee: Do we have the raw logs to validate?
[15:31] Priya Raman: Yes, we'll share compressed logs and an analysis spreadsheet. Note: some labels are old (see disclaimer).
[15:40] Diego Ruiz: For the fallback path you mentioned, how automatic is the routing? Can we require manual approval?
[15:45] Avery Chen: It's policy-based. You can pick fully automatic (recommended for traffic-critical paths) or semi-automatic with an approval webhook. Many customers start semi-automatic for first week of canary.
[15:59] Sana Patel: On data residency / compliance — in case we trigger fallback to a model in another region, what does that do to data residency?
[16:06] Priya Raman: Good question. Redwood's routing policy can enforce region constraints; fallback to other region only if you enable multi-region routing policy. If you need strict residency, we can restrict routes to the same region or use Private deployment.
[16:26] Marcus Lee: For the canary timeline — we want to ship a canary that adjusts batching window and watermark. Proposed timeline?
[16:31] Avery Chen: Proposed: this week — Redwood enables prefix caching on staging and shares config. Customer runs quantized variant by Wed. Next Tue morning run a 2-hour canary to 2% of traffic at 07:30 PST. Then ramp to 20% over next two days if metrics look good.
[16:50] Priya Raman: We'll also provide a dashboard link with pre-configured alerts: p95 > 800ms, error rate > 0.5%, queue depth > 50.
[17:00] Marcus Lee: Can you put sample alert thresholds in the follow-up email?
[17:03] Avery Chen: Yes.
[17:05] [minor audio artifact]
[17:25] Diego Ruiz: Network question again — do you need us to open any special ports for Private?
[17:29] Priya Raman: If you go Private, we need access for control-plane to push configs; it's a standard egress to Redwood's control endpoint, or you can do an air-gapped manual sync. We'll put the network diagram in the doc.
[18:00] Sana Patel: For evals — we'll run our long-context regressions on the quantized model. If we see >2% quality delta we'll halt the fallback path.
[18:12] Priya Raman: Sounds reasonable. We'll include rollback policies.
[18:25] Marcus Lee: What about token billing when fallback triggers to quantized model? Any difference?
[18:29] Priya Raman: Quantized model generally reduces costs per token slightly due to faster kernel throughput, but billing is per-token across variants — we'll show unit economics including tokens/sec and GPU hours.
[18:47] Avery Chen: Ok, let's recap next steps verbally before action items: Redwood to share micro-bench + config snippets; Riverbend to run quantized tests; both to align on canary schedule and alert thresholds.
[19:05] Marcus Lee: Agreed.
[19:08] Priya Raman: Any other questions?
[19:12] Sana Patel: One thing — can Redwood show a sample of batch-size distribution visualization? That helped last time.
[19:18] Priya Raman: Yes, will include that.
[19:22] Diego Ruiz: Also, small ask — could you annotate logs with request route IDs so we can map our upstream traces?
[19:29] Priya Raman: Absolutely. We'll add request-route-id metadata to the log schema.
[19:36] [crackle]
[25:00] Priya Raman: (walkthrough) Looking at the spike timeline, you can see three correlated signals: queue depth, batch size variance, and the GPU utilization bump. When those peak together, tail latency spikes. So if we keep queue depth under the watermark and raise KV hits, we smooth the curve.
[27:30] Marcus Lee: If we reduce batching window to 10ms, what batch size should we expect?
[27:34] Priya Raman: For your waveform, expect avg batch size 6-8, tokens/sec may dip ~8% but p95 will fall by ~20-30% — good trade for UX-sensitive flows.
[28:05] Sana Patel: We'll test both 12ms and 10ms windows.
[28:10] Avery Chen: For the micro-bench we'll provide flags: --batch-window-ms, --adaptive, --queue-watermark, --quantized-variant.
[28:22] Marcus Lee: One last question on telemetry retention — if we increase retention to 30 days for debugging, any cost impacts?
[28:28] Priya Raman: Yes, small bump. We'll include retention cost in the delta sheet.
[28:34] Diego Ruiz: Okay that covers my infra questions.
[28:38] [silence 5s]
[35:00] Avery Chen: Wrapping: I'll send follow-up with artifacts: micro-benchmark repo, config snippet, KV cache suggestion, eval report link, and cost delta. Priya will draft concurrency yaml. Customer to run quantized sweep and respond by 12/15.
[35:23] Marcus Lee: Thanks — sounds good.
[35:28] Sana Patel: Thanks everyone.
[35:31] Diego Ruiz: Thanks.
[35:33] Priya Raman: Thanks all.
